semantics.note: 'I expect' and 'there will be' are unhedged, so this is a scored forecast. The growth clause is kept as the antecedent. No deadline was given. The later 'perhaps many more' passage is a separate, hedged statement and is not part of this claim.

contract.note: Requiring both mental and physical harm is a fair plain reading of 'mental and physical health'. Requiring injuries that the advice actually contributed to, not just risky answers, is also fair. The early-resolution rule is demanding but fits a forecast with no deadline.

evidence.note: Company disclosure of ChatGPT adoption growth through 2025. It establishes the antecedent, not the outcome.
Microsoft's May 2023 disclosure of large Bing chat use. It supports the antecedent only.
Physicians rated 5–13% of simulated answers as unsafe. This supports repeated deficient advice but shows potential harm, not actual injury.

Clinical-record preprint finding 28 patients whose psychosis worsened after AI interactions, in records to April 2026. It supports the mental-health part but has no chat logs and says nothing about physical harm.
Report of bromism after alleged ChatGPT advice. There were no chat logs and the authors call the link speculation. The injury date is not given, so it cannot be the decisive dated physical injury.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent is met, and repeated deficient advice plus some documented mental-health worsening are shown. The physical-injury part rests only on the bromism case, which has no logs and no dated clinical link, so the early-resolution rule is not jointly met. The forecast has no deadline, and the missing proof is not a failure. It stays unresolved.

semantics.note: A factual claim about which model powered the Belgian case. The side remark about erroneous headlines is rightly left unscored.

contract.note: Reading GPT-J as the model family behind Chai's fine-tuned model is the ordinary sense of what Marcus wrote.

evidence.note: VICE report of 30 March 2023 quoting Chai's founders: the app's model is based on GPT-J and was then fine-tuned. It ties the case to Chai's Eliza. The founders are the developer, which the contract accepts as a source.

reviews.rationale: Contemporary reporting quoting the developer says the Eliza chatbot ran on a GPT-J-based model, not on OpenAI's GPT-3 or ChatGPT. That matches the claim under the contract's model-family reading. Nothing in the packet contradicts it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his FAQ answer.

semantics.note: A present-tense observation about public trust, plus a broad risk clause. 'Huge' fairly paraphrases 'immense'.

contract.note: Reading 'immense' as a large share, not necessarily a majority, is an ordinary reading, though slightly generous. Measuring stated trust in the quarter before publication is reasonable. The result depends on whether about 30% of US adults counts as immense.

evidence.note: Marist national poll, 20–23 March 2023: 30% of US adults trust ChatGPT-type information a great deal or a good amount. That is a large absolute group, though 68% expressed little or no trust.
GPT-4 system card from March 2023 names overreliance on wrong outputs as a concrete risk. It is OpenAI's own disclosure, but it is relevant to the risk clause.

reviews.rationale: In March 2023 about 30% of US adults, tens of millions of people, said they trusted ChatGPT-type outputs. That fits 'an immense segment' on a plain reading. The contemporary GPT-4 system card documents the risk of overreliance. Most respondents did not trust the outputs, and that limits the claim but does not contradict it.
